objectives: Set up Denavit-Hartenberg parameters for a serial arm.
Compose homogeneous transforms to compute end-effector pose.
Use the Jacobian for velocity, singularities, and inverse kinematics.

slides.title: Denavit-Hartenberg, homogeneous transforms, and the forward map
slides.body:
**Kinematics** treats motion without forces. **Forward kinematics (FK)**: given joint angles θ = (θ₁, ..., θₙ), compute end-effector pose T = (position, orientation). **Inverse kinematics (IK)**: given a desired T, solve for θ.

FK is the easy direction (one function evaluation). IK is hard (multiple solutions, possibly none, possibly infinitely many).

**Homogeneous transformation matrix** — the central object:
$$T = \begin{bmatrix} R & p \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \in SE(3)$$
where R ∈ SO(3) is a 3×3 rotation matrix (R Rᵀ = I, det R = +1) and p ∈ ℝ³ is the translation. Composition is matrix multiplication: T₀² = T₀¹ T₁². Homogeneous coordinates extend points to (x, y, z, 1) so that translation becomes linear.

**Denavit-Hartenberg (DH) parameters (Jacques Denavit + Richard Hartenberg, 1955)**: a canonical four-parameter convention for placing coordinate frames on a serial chain. For each link i:
- **aᵢ** (link length): distance along x̂ᵢ from ẑᵢ to ẑᵢ₊₁.
- **αᵢ** (link twist): angle about x̂ᵢ from ẑᵢ to ẑᵢ₊₁.
- **dᵢ** (link offset): distance along ẑᵢ from x̂ᵢ₋₁ to x̂ᵢ.
- **θᵢ** (joint angle): angle about ẑᵢ from x̂ᵢ₋₁ to x̂ᵢ.

For a revolute joint θᵢ varies; for prismatic, dᵢ varies. The link transform is:
$$T_{i-1}^i = R_z(\theta_i) \cdot \text{Trans}_z(d_i) \cdot \text{Trans}_x(a_i) \cdot R_x(\alpha_i)$$

The full FK is the product:
$$T_0^n(\theta) = T_0^1(\theta_1) \, T_1^2(\theta_2) \, \cdots \, T_{n-1}^n(\theta_n)$$

There are two DH conventions — *classical* (above, frame i fixed to link i with z along joint i+1) and *modified DH* (Craig 1986; frame i with z along joint i). Most modern textbooks (Craig, Spong, Lynch-Park) use modified; ROS URDF uses an explicit transform per joint that subsumes DH.

**Product-of-exponentials (PoE, Brockett 1984)**: alternative formulation using twists ξ ∈ se(3) and matrix exponentials:
$$T(\theta) = e^{\hat{\xi}_1 \theta_1} e^{\hat{\xi}_2 \theta_2} \cdots e^{\hat{\xi}_n \theta_n} M$$
with M the zero-configuration pose. Used in the modern Lynch-Park textbook because it doesn't require attaching frames to each link — only choose a base + reference pose.

**Rotation representations** (each with tradeoffs):
- Rotation matrix R: 9 parameters, 6 constraints; unique; gimbal-free; standard for computation.
- Euler angles (roll-pitch-yaw, ZYX, ZYZ, ...): 3 parameters; intuitive; gimbal lock at singularities.
- Axis-angle (ω̂, θ): 4 parameters; closest to exponential coordinates.
- Quaternion q = (w, x, y, z): 4 parameters, 1 constraint (|q|=1); smooth; no gimbal lock; used in graphics, control, ROS tf2.
- Modified Rodrigues parameters, exponential coordinates ωθ ∈ ℝ³: 3-parameter, minimal.

**Try it**: the visualization below lets you drag joint angles and watch the end-effector trace through the workspace.

slides.title: Interactive: forward kinematics of a 3R arm
slides.body:
Drag the joint sliders to see how (θ₁, θ₂, θ₃) map to end-effector position. This is a planar 3R arm with link lengths (1, 1, 0.7). Notice:

- **Multiple joint configurations** can produce the same end-effector pose ("elbow up" vs "elbow down" — IK has multiple solutions).
- The **reachable workspace** is an annulus: outer radius L₁+L₂+L₃ = 2.7, inner radius depends on joint limits and self-collision.
- At the **outer boundary** the arm is fully extended — small task-space motions require huge joint changes (singularity).
- Try setting θ₂ = 0: the arm is straight. Differential motion at the tip requires the wrist to swing dramatically — this is the **boundary singularity**.

The transform composition under the hood is exactly:
$$T_0^3(\theta) = T_0^1(\theta_1) T_1^2(\theta_2) T_2^3(\theta_3)$$
With each Tᵢ₋₁ⁱ a rotation by θᵢ followed by translation along link length Lᵢ.

This is the simplest non-trivial robot. Real arms (Kuka, Franka, Universal Robots UR5/UR10, ABB) have 6 or 7 revolutes in 3D and the same logic generalizes — just bigger matrices.

slides.title: Jacobian, singularities, manipulability, inverse kinematics
slides.body:
**Jacobian** J(θ): the linear map from joint velocities to end-effector velocities.
$$\dot{x} = J(\theta) \dot{\theta} \quad ; \quad J \in \mathbb{R}^{6 \times n}$$
The top three rows give linear velocity v ∈ ℝ³; the bottom three give angular velocity ω ∈ ℝ³. Two flavors:
- **Geometric Jacobian**: rows correspond to physical twist coordinates (most common).
- **Analytical Jacobian**: derivative of a minimal parameterization (Euler-angle rates); has artificial singularities at gimbal lock.

**Computing J**: column i of the geometric Jacobian for a revolute joint is (ẑᵢ × (pₙ - pᵢ), ẑᵢ); for a prismatic joint it is (ẑᵢ, 0). Closed form via DH/PoE.

**Static force transpose**: the Jacobian transpose maps end-effector wrenches to joint torques: τ = Jᵀ F. This is the principle of virtual work; foundational for impedance control + force feedback.

**Singularities**: configurations where J loses rank — the end-effector cannot move in some direction without infinite joint velocity.
- **Boundary singularity**: arm fully extended (workspace boundary).
- **Internal singularity**: e.g., wrist singularity when two joint axes align (PUMA: joints 4 and 6 collinear when θ₅ = 0).
- Detected by det J = 0 (for square J) or smallest singular value of J approaching 0.
- Cause IK to fail, generate large torques, motion-planning failures.

**Manipulability ellipsoid (Yoshikawa 1985)**: visualize J Jᵀ as an ellipsoid; principal axes = singular vectors, lengths = singular values. **Manipulability index** w = √det(J Jᵀ). w → 0 at singularities. Used for posture optimization in redundant arms.

**Inverse kinematics — analytical**:
- **Pieper's principle (Donald Pieper, Stanford, 1968)**: if three consecutive joint axes intersect at a point (e.g., a spherical wrist), closed-form IK exists. Most industrial arms (PUMA, Stäubli, Kuka classical) satisfy this.
- **Up to 8 solutions** for a 6R arm with spherical wrist (shoulder left/right, elbow up/down, wrist flip).
- Closed-form is fast (microseconds) + exact + lets you choose among solutions deterministically.
- IKFast (Diankov) and analytic solvers ship with MoveIt.

**Inverse kinematics — numerical**:
- **Newton-Raphson**: iterate θₖ₊₁ = θₖ + J⁺(x_target - x(θₖ)). Local convergence near a solution.
- **Damped least squares (DLS, Levenberg-Marquardt)** — Nakamura + Hanafusa 1986; Wampler 1986:
  $$\Delta\theta = J^T (J J^T + \lambda^2 I)^{-1} \Delta x$$
  Damping λ regularizes near singularities; trades accuracy for stability.
- **Pseudoinverse** J⁺ = Jᵀ(J Jᵀ)⁻¹ (when J full row rank) — Moore-Penrose inverse; minimum-norm joint motion.
- **Optimization-based**: minimize ||x(θ) - x_target||² + regularizers over θ; SQP, gradient descent. TRAC-IK (Beeson + Ames 2015) combines Newton + SQP.
- **Learning-based**: neural-network IK for redundancy resolution + style imitation (recent).

**Redundancy resolution** (n > task DOF):
- Null-space projection: θ̇ = J⁺ ẋ + (I - J⁺J) q̇₀, where q̇₀ is a secondary-task gradient (manipulability, joint centering, obstacle avoidance).
- Khatib's **task-priority** framework: stack tasks, each in null space of higher ones. **Operational-space control (OSC)** uses this for whole-body humanoid control.

This machinery generalizes to mobile manipulators, parallel mechanisms, soft robots (with infinite-dimensional configuration), and humanoids (floating-base + contact constraints). Software: KDL, Pinocchio (INRIA — Carpentier et al.), Drake, ROS MoveIt, IKFast.

question.question: Derive forward + inverse kinematics for a planar 2R arm
question.goal: Two revolute joints in a plane, link lengths L₁ and L₂. Given (θ₁, θ₂), find end-effector (x, y). Then solve the inverse.

steps.prompt: Write the forward kinematics (x, y) as functions of θ₁, θ₂.

acceptedAnswers: x = L1 cos θ1 + L2 cos(θ1 + θ2); y = L1 sin θ1 + L2 sin(θ1 + θ2)
x = L1 cos(θ1) + L2 cos(θ1+θ2), y = L1 sin(θ1) + L2 sin(θ1+θ2)

hints: Sum of two vectors: first link in θ₁ direction, second link in (θ₁+θ₂) direction.
steps.reveal: x = L₁ cos θ₁ + L₂ cos(θ₁+θ₂); y = L₁ sin θ₁ + L₂ sin(θ₁+θ₂). Direct sum of two link displacements.

steps.prompt: For IK, first solve for θ₂. Use the identity x² + y² = L₁² + L₂² + 2 L₁ L₂ cos θ₂.

acceptedAnswers: cos θ2 = (x² + y² − L1² − L2²) / (2 L1 L2)

hints: Squaring + summing the FK equations eliminates θ₁.
steps.reveal: cos θ₂ = (x² + y² − L₁² − L₂²) / (2 L₁ L₂). Two solutions: θ₂ = ±acos(...) (elbow up + elbow down). No real solution if |cos θ₂| > 1 → target out of reach.

steps.prompt: Now solve for θ₁ given θ₂.

acceptedAnswers: θ1 = atan2(y, x) − atan2(L2 sin θ2, L1 + L2 cos θ2)
θ1 = atan2(y,x) - atan2(L2 sinθ2, L1 + L2 cosθ2)

hints: θ₁ = atan2(y, x) − atan2(L₂ sin θ₂, L₁ + L₂ cos θ₂).
steps.reveal: θ₁ = atan2(y, x) − atan2(L₂ sin θ₂, L₁ + L₂ cos θ₂). The first term aims the arm at the target; the second subtracts the offset due to bending at the elbow. Use atan2 to handle all four quadrants.

steps.prompt: When is the IK undefined or singular?

acceptedAnswers: out of reach when sqrt(x²+y²) > L1+L2 or < |L1-L2|; singular when θ2 = 0 or π

steps.reveal: Out of reach (no solution): √(x²+y²) > L₁+L₂ or < |L₁−L₂|. Boundary singularity: θ₂ = 0 (fully extended) or π (folded); Jacobian rank-deficient; small task-space motion → large joint changes.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\theta_2 = \pm\arccos\left(\frac{x^2+y^2-L_1^2-L_2^2}{2L_1 L_2}\right);\; \theta_1 = \operatorname{atan2}(y,x) - \operatorname{atan2}(L_2 \sin\theta_2, L_1+L_2 \cos\theta_2)}$$ The planar 2R is the simplest non-trivial IK and exhibits all the qualitative phenomena: multiple solutions, unreachable regions, boundary singularities. Pieper showed that any 6R arm with a spherical wrist admits an analogous closed-form IK; this is why classical industrial arms are designed that way.

question.question: Why does damped least squares (Nakamura + Hanafusa 1986; Wampler 1986) outperform the plain pseudoinverse for IK near singularities?
options: Near a singularity, smallest singular value of J → 0; pseudoinverse J⁺ = Jᵀ(JJᵀ)⁻¹ blows up → arbitrarily large joint velocities. DLS replaces (JJᵀ)⁻¹ with (JJᵀ + λ²I)⁻¹: the damping λ² lower-bounds the smallest eigenvalue, so joint velocities stay finite. Tradeoff: tracking error grows as λ increases, but the controller stays stable + executable on hardware. Standard in MoveIt, OpenRAVE, modern IK solvers.
question.explanation: Pseudoinverse diverges at singularities; damped least squares regularizes via (JJᵀ + λ²I)⁻¹, trading tracking accuracy for boundedness. This is the workhorse numerical IK approach since the mid-1980s.

slides.workedSolution: Plain pseudoinverse fails at singularities because (JJᵀ)⁻¹ becomes ill-conditioned. DLS adds λ²I inside the inverse: bounded velocities at cost of tracking accuracy. Choose λ as function of smallest singular value (variable damping) or constant. Standard since Nakamura-Hanafusa + Wampler (1986).

question.question: Using 7-DOF redundancy
question.prompt: A surgeon's robot has a 7-DOF arm and a 6-DOF task (knot tying near a patient's chest with cameras + retractors crowding the workspace). Explain how null-space (redundancy) resolution lets you pick joint configurations that (a) avoid colliding with the cameras, (b) stay far from joint limits, and (c) maximize manipulability — all simultaneously, using a task-priority stack à la Khatib.

question.question: Planar 2R arm with L₁ = L₂ = 1. At θ₁ = π/2, θ₂ = 0, what is the determinant of the 2×2 Jacobian (relating joint to Cartesian velocity)?
question.hint: θ₂ = 0 is fully extended — boundary singularity.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain the relationship between forward kinematics, inverse kinematics, the Jacobian, singularities, and manipulability — and why redundancy is a feature.
question.rubric: Mentions FK as a function θ → T (cheap, deterministic); IK as the inverse (multiple solutions, possibly none, expensive); the Jacobian J = ∂x/∂θ (linear approximation of FK; maps joint velocities to end-effector velocities); singularities as configurations where rank(J) drops (end-effector can't move in some direction without infinite joint velocity; boundary + internal types); manipulability w = √det(JJᵀ) as a scalar measure of distance from singularity; redundancy (n_joints > n_task) creating a null space that allows secondary objectives (obstacle avoidance, manipulability, joint-limit avoidance) while still satisfying the primary task — via Khatib's operational-space / task-priority framework. Notes Pieper's principle for analytic IK + DLS (Nakamura/Hanafusa, Wampler) for numerical IK.
